paras: The exclusion of Black horse handlers from the Elwood, Indiana, street fair took place in August 1903, when Black men caring for horses entered in the fair's horse show told their white employers they did not dare enter the town because they had been warned to stay away. Local authorities told the horsemen that no Black person had ever been allowed in Elwood, and the story spread through white newspapers as an example of a Northern town that barred Black people.

Elwood, a factory town in Indiana, was preparing a street fair with a horse show for the week after Aug. 15, 1903. A month earlier, a Jeffersonville column in the Louisville Courier-Journal had described John Lawson, a house boy sentenced to the Reformatory for robbing a saloon, as "the only colored resident of Elwood."

Several horsemen with animals entered in the show had brought Black employees to care for the horses, described in one version as "hostlers, riders and drivers." These men told their employers that they did not dare enter the town, as they had been "warned not to approach the place"; the Richmond Times Dispatch said they had been "solemnly warned." The coverage does not say who gave the warning or how it was delivered.

The horsemen then went to the local authorities, who told them that the people of Elwood, "and especially the employees of the factories," were "greatly prejudiced against negroes" and that no Black person had ever been allowed to come into the town. According to the Times Dispatch, the horsemen "could get no satisfaction" from the officials, who said that "the rule would not be resolved" [as printed].
No report of arrests, of any official action against those who issued the warning, or of whether the handlers attended the fair was found.

The story reached print through an Indianapolis dispatch dated Aug. 15, which the New York Sun ran the next day under the headline "No Negroes Wanted There," with a subhead saying Black people were "Barred Out of Elwood, Ind., by the Employees of Factories." The Alexandria Gazette carried the same text as "Negroes Excluded" on Aug. 17, and the Richmond Times Dispatch printed a rewritten version on Aug. 18. These papers presented the exclusion as a curiosity, "one town in the country" where a Black person would not be allowed within the town limits, without editorial comment.

Southern editorial writers took up the item as evidence of Northern prejudice. A Morgantown, West Virginia, paper noted on Aug. 21 that the town where "no negroes are allowed" was "not in the South," and the squib was repeated in West Virginia and Florida weeklies over the following week. The Manning Times of South Carolina, citing The State, called Elwood "another northern town which will not allow a negro in its limits" and closed, "And this is in Gov. Durbin's commonwealth!"; the Marlboro Democrat reprinted the item two days later. In Olympia, the Washington Standard compared Elwood's "utter exclusion" of Black people to Tacoma's treatment of the Chinese and asked whether the "party of virtue and morality" ought to "reconstruct the North."
No report of the episode was found in the Black press or in Indiana papers.

Versions of the dispatch differ slightly on the officials' words, with the Sun reporting that no Black person "had ever been allowed" in town and the Alexandria Gazette that none "is allowed." The claim of total exclusion came from local officials and was not tested in the coverage, although the July item about John Lawson describes one Black resident of the town.

reader.title: Exclusion of Black horse handlers from the Elwood, Indiana, street fair
bases: Black handlers were warned not to approach Elwood and stayed out, and officials described a standing rule of exclusion; no assault, removal of residents or property damage is reported (A2, A3, A4).
Every account goes back to one Indianapolis dispatch of Aug. 15 (A2, A3, A4), and the later items quote or comment on it (A6, A5, A11); no local Elwood report or independent account was found.
